title: How can Gumulgal number names do all four operations?
description: The Gumulgal number names are carried past six by counting in twos. The video adds, subtracts, multiplies and divides four given numbers using only the words ukasar and urapon, and checks each answer with ordinary number words.
teaching_notes: One idea: a number counted in twos is a row of ukasar with an urapon at the end if one is left over, and two urapon make one more ukasar. Each operation works on the row of words. Watch for students who convert to Hindu numerals before they begin.

source: Figure it Out (early number systems, question 2)
video_script.why: The child works with the Gumulgal names built from twos, the same way as the solved example, and carries them beyond six to compute.
video_script.substitution: Treat each number as a row of ukasar with perhaps an urapon, then join, take away, double or share the rows.
video_script.anchor: four Gumulgal expressions, each written as a row of the words ukasar and urapon
video_script.payoff_line: Each answer is a row of ukasar, with an urapon only when one is left over

final_answer.value: (i) ukasar written 8 times (ii) ukasar-urapon (iii) ukasar written 18 times (iv) ukasar-ukasar
final_answer.spoken: part one is ukasar written eight times, part two is ukasar-urapon, part three is ukasar written eighteen times, and part four is ukasar-ukasar

hold_back: (i) ukasar written 8 times (ii) ukasar-urapon (iii) ukasar written 18 times (iv) ukasar-ukasar
never_show: the answer card before the last beat of the board solution
maths_rules: urapon is 1 and ukasar is 2; counting goes on in 2s past 6
(i) 4 ukasar + urapon = 9 and 3 ukasar + urapon = 7; joining gives 7 ukasar and 2 urapon, and 2 urapon make 1 ukasar, so 8 ukasar = 16
(ii) 4 ukasar + urapon minus 3 ukasar leaves ukasar + urapon = 3, and 9 − 6 = 3
(iii) ukasar-ukasar is 2 + 2 = 4; doubling twice: 9 × 2 = 18 = 9 ukasar, then 18 × 2 = 36 = 18 ukasar
(iv) 8 ukasar = 16; groups of ukasar-ukasar hold 2 ukasar each, so 8 ukasar make 4 groups, which is ukasar-ukasar; 16 ÷ 4 = 4
video_script.design: One idea: do each operation on the rows of words, then check with ordinary numbers. The four rows stay on the stage and each step acts on one of them.

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about the Gumulgal number system carried on past six. Counting goes on in twos.
<bookmark mark='rows'/>Here are four tasks, one for each operation.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>How can we add, subtract, multiply and divide using only the Gumulgal words, with no Hindu numerals?

beats.on_screen: the four rows hold still and the question mark glows

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board and the question mark glows

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: the four rows move to the stage; a pebble row shows urapon as one pebble and ukasar as a pair; two urapon are shown joining into one ukasar

marks.words: a pebble shows urapon as one and a pair of pebbles shows ukasar as two
marks.join: two single pebbles join into one pair, so two urapon make one ukasar

narration: <bookmark mark='words'/>Urapon is one and ukasar is two. A number is a row of ukasar, with an urapon at the end if one is left over.
<bookmark mark='join'/>Two urapon pebbles join together, and they make one more ukasar.

beats.on_screen: Given: (i) 4 ukasar + urapon plus 3 ukasar + urapon; (ii) 4 ukasar + urapon minus 3 ukasar; (iii) 4 ukasar + urapon times ukasar-ukasar; (iv) 8 ukasar divided by ukasar-ukasar

marks.given: the four tasks are written as the given

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, four tasks, with an add, a subtract, a multiply and a divide, all in Gumulgal words.

beats.on_screen: To find: the answer to each task, as a row of Gumulgal words

marks.find: the words To find are written under the given

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find each answer as a row of Gumulgal words.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: (i) join the words: 4 ukasar + 3 ukasar = 7 ukasar; the 2 urapon make 1 more ukasar; so 8 ukasar

marks.m1: the two rows slide together and join into one row, with seven ukasar and two urapon
marks.m2: the two urapon pebbles join into a pair, and the row now shows eight ukasar

narration: <bookmark mark='s1'/>Step one, part one, add the two numbers.
<bookmark mark='m1'/>Join the words. Four ukasar and three ukasar make seven ukasar. We also have two urapon.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The two urapon make one more ukasar. That gives eight ukasar.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: (ii) take 3 ukasar away from 4 ukasar and an urapon; ukasar-urapon is left

marks.m3: three ukasar slide away from the row of four ukasar and an urapon, and one ukasar and the urapon stay glowing

narration: <bookmark mark='s2'/>Step two, part two, subtract.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Take three ukasar away from four ukasar and an urapon. One ukasar and the urapon are left. That is ukasar-urapon.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: (iii) ukasar-ukasar is two twos, so double the first number twice: 4 ukasar + urapon, doubled, is 9 ukasar; doubled again, 18 ukasar

marks.m4: the row is doubled: eight ukasar and two urapon appear, and the two urapon join into one ukasar, giving nine ukasar
marks.m5: the row of nine ukasar is doubled again and shows eighteen ukasar

narration: <bookmark mark='s3'/>Step three, part three, multiply by ukasar-ukasar.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>Ukasar-ukasar is two twos. Double the first number, and then double the result. Doubling gives eight ukasar and two urapon, which is nine ukasar.
<bookmark mark='m5'/>Double again, and the row grows to eighteen ukasar.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: (iv) share 8 ukasar into groups of ukasar-ukasar: 4 groups, written ukasar-ukasar

marks.m6: the eight ukasar are lifted out in groups, two ukasar to a group, and four groups form
marks.m7: the four groups are counted in twos and written as ukasar-ukasar

narration: <bookmark mark='s4'/>Step four, part four, divide.
<bookmark mark='m6'/>Make groups of ukasar-ukasar. Each group holds two ukasar, so eight ukasar fill four groups.
<bookmark mark='m7'/>The number of groups is four, and four is written ukasar-ukasar.

beats.on_screen: Step 5: check with ordinary numbers: 9 + 7 = 16 = 8 ukasar; 9 − 6 = 3; 9 × 4 = 36 = 18 ukasar; 16 ÷ 4 = 4

marks.m8: the first number reads nine and the second reads seven, and the sum reads sixteen, which is eight ukasar
marks.m9: nine take six leaves three, and nine times four makes thirty six, which is eighteen ukasar
marks.m10: sixteen shared into fours gives four, which is ukasar-ukasar

narration: <bookmark mark='s5'/>Step five, put the answers back using ordinary numbers.
<bookmark mark='m8'/>Four ukasar and an urapon is nine, and three ukasar and an urapon is seven. Nine and seven make sixteen, which is eight ukasar.
<bookmark mark='m9'/>Nine take away six is three, which is ukasar-urapon. Nine times four is thirty six, which is eighteen ukasar.
<bookmark mark='m10'/>Sixteen shared into groups of four gives four, which is ukasar-ukasar.

beats.on_screen: Answer: (i) ukasar written 8 times (ii) ukasar-urapon (iii) ukasar written 18 times (iv) ukasar-ukasar
